components.note: ⺼ (flesh) marks a body part.
佥 (qiān) gives a rough sound hint; the traditional form 臉 has the same part.

example.fact: 脸 is the face as a body part and also 'face' in the social sense: 丢脸 (lose face), 不要脸 (shameless) and 给面子 are close cousins of this idea. It takes the measure word 张 (一张脸) and appears in 洗脸 (wash one's face) and 笑脸 (smiling face).

components.note: 千 (thousand) suggests a great quantity or weight.
里 (mile) suggests distance, so the pair is often explained as a burden carried a long way.

example.fact: 重 has two main readings: zhòng ('heavy, serious', as here and in 重要, 严重) and chóng ('again, to repeat', as in 重新, 重复). Tone and meaning change with the reading, so look at the context: 重来 (chónglái) means 'do over'.

components.note: 心 (heart) shows a kindly feeling.
因 (yīn) gives a loose sound hint; the finals are close.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǒngyuǎn jìde nǐ de ēnqíng.
example.english: I will always remember your kindness.
example.fact: 恩 is a formal, warm word for benevolence, seen in 恩人 (benefactor), 感恩 (be grateful) and 恩爱 (loving, said of couples). 感恩节 is the Chinese name for Thanksgiving.

components.note: 曰 (to say, here the lower part) is the base; the shape is old, and its link to 'once' is a later borrowing, so treat the whole as one unit.

example.fact: 曾 is nearly always seen as 曾经 ('once, previously'), which is used with 过 to talk about past experiences, as in 我曾经去过北京. It is also a surname (read Zēng), which is the reading in names like 曾国藩.

components.note: Picture of an elephant with its trunk and legs, rotated sideways; the modern shape is a heavily reduced version of that picture.

example.pinyin: Dòngwùyuán lǐ yǒu yì tóu xiàng.
example.english: There is an elephant in the zoo.
example.fact: 象 is 'elephant' on its own (usually 大象) and also 'appearance' in 印象 (impression), 现象 (phenomenon), 想象 (imagine) and 对象 (target, partner). 象 and 像 are often confused: 像 means 'like' or 'to resemble'.

components.note: 衣 (clothes) shows the original sense of dress.
壮 (zhuàng) gives the sound; the two differ only in the initial.

example.english: He is pretending to be asleep.
example.fact: 装 has many uses: 'to pack/load' (装箱子), 'to install' (安装), 'to pretend' (装傻, 装睡), and 'clothes' (服装, 西装). It's a good example of how one character can mix 'putting on' clothes and 'putting on' an act.

components.note: 氵 (water) is the left part, pointing to something that flows along a set course.
去 (to go) is on the right, giving the idea of a course that is followed, which fits 'method' and 'law'.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǒu yí gè hǎo bànfǎ.
example.fact: 法 is law (法律, 犯法) and also 'method' (办法, 方法, 想法). It is the character in 法国 (France) and 法语 (French), as 法 alone refers to France, derived from the old transliteration.

components.note: 禾 (grain) represents the crop.
子 (child, seed) is the seed or the youngest, so the character is linked to a crop's season.

example.pinyin: Chūnjì shì zuì hǎo de jìjié.
example.fact: 季 is mostly seen in 季节 (season), 四季 (the four seasons) and 季度 (quarter of a year), and compounds like 旺季 (peak season). It is also a surname.

components.note: 亻 (person) shows that it concerns a person.
吏 (an official) is the one who sends and directs others, which fits the sense of 'cause' or 'order'.

example.pinyin: Zhège xiāoxi shǐ wǒ hěn gāoxìng.
example.english: This news made me very happy.
example.fact: 使 is a causative verb in written Chinese, as in 使…高兴 ('make … happy'). It also means 'to use' in 使用 and 'envoy' in 大使 (ambassador). In casual speech 让 (ràng) is often used instead of 使.

components.note: 车 (cart) reflects wheels turning.
专 (zhuān) gives the sound; the finals are the same.

example.fact: 转 has two readings: zhuǎn ('to turn, to transfer', as in 转弯 and 转学) and zhuàn ('to rotate, to wander', as in 转圈 and 转来转去). With 转 + noun it also means to forward things: 转发 (forward a message).

components.note: 一 (a line) is repeated twice.
The second 一 completes the pair, so the character is just two lines for 'two'.

example.fact: 二 is used for counting and in numbers (二十, 第二), but before a measure word Chinese uses 两 instead: 两个人, not 二个人. Mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes for learners.

components.note: 弓 (bow) hints at strength and power.
虽 (suī) is a visual part; the sound connection is loose.

example.fact: 强 has the readings qiáng ('strong'), qiǎng ('to force', as in 勉强) and jiàng ('stubborn', as in 倔强). The strong reading shows up in 加强 (strengthen), 强大 (powerful), and 强调 (emphasise).

components.note: 牛 (ox) shows that it was originally about a bull, a special animal for sacrifice.
寺 (sì) gives a rough sound hint; the finals are close.

example.fact: 特 means 'special' and 'especially': 特别 (special, very), 特点 (feature), 特色 (distinctive character) and 特地 (specially). It is also common in transliterations, as in 特朗普 (Trump).

components.note: 艹 (grass) shows that old medicines were herbs.
约 (yuē) gives the sound; the finals are close.

example.english: You should take your medicine on time.
example.fact: 药 uses the verb 吃 in Chinese ('eat medicine'), and appears in 药店 (pharmacy), 药片 (tablet) and 药方 (prescription). It is also the root of 火药 (gunpowder), which is literally 'fire medicine'.

components.note: 皿 (a vessel) is the bowl that holds the liquid.
丿 (a drop) is the drop of blood in the bowl, a sacrificial offering.

example.fact: 血 has two readings: xuè (in compounds and formal speech, as in 血液, 流血, 血型) and xiě (colloquially alone, as in 吐血 or 一口血). Both are heard, and the same character is also used in 热血 (passion).

components.note: 亻 (person) shows that a person is hurt.

example.fact: 伤 is a noun (伤口, wound) and a verb ('to hurt'), as in 伤心 (heartbroken) and 受伤 (to get injured). It also means 'to harm', as in 伤害.

components.note: 忄 (heart) points to feelings of puzzlement.
The right-hand part is the sound clue in the simplified shape, but the match is loose.

example.fact: 怪 means 'strange' in 奇怪 and 怪不得 ('no wonder'), and 'to blame' in 别怪我 ('don't blame me'). Used as an adverb in 怪好看的 it means 'rather' (colloquial, northern).

components.note: 讠 (speech) shows reading aloud.
卖 (mài) is the right part, and sound link is loose; it comes from the old 賣.

example.fact: 读 is to read aloud and to study: 读书 (read books, or go to school), 读音 (pronunciation) and 阅读 (reading). Note 读 is read dòu in the rare word 句读 (punctuation).

components.note: 目 (eye) shows looking.
焦 (jiāo) gives the sound; the finals are the same.

example.fact: 瞧 is a colloquial word for 'look', used mostly in northern speech: 瞧一瞧 (have a look) and 瞧不起 (look down on). It's less formal than 看.

components.note: Looks like half of 木 (tree): the right half of the trunk is cut away, leaving a thin slice.

example.pinyin: Qǐng gěi wǒ yí piàn miànbāo.
example.english: Please give me a slice of bread.
example.fact: 片 is a measure word for flat things (一片叶子, 一片面包) and a noun for film or cards: 电影片, 照片 (photo), 名片 (business card). In 片 as 'film' it can also read piān in 片儿 (a flat piece, spoken).

components.note: 灬 (fire) is the bottom part, showing soot.
The top part is a chimney or window shape, so the picture reads as something blackened by fire and smoke.

example.fact: 黑 means 'black' and 'dark', as in 黑夜 (night), 黑板 (blackboard), and slang like 黑客 (hacker) and 黑名单 (blacklist). It can also be used of 'illegal': 黑车 (unlicensed car).

components.note: Picture of a person with a rounded belly, which shows the torso; the original sense was a pregnant body.

example.fact: 身 is body, as in 身体, 身高 (height) and 身份 (identity), and also a measure word for suits of clothes: 一身衣服. In 身上 it means 'on one's person'.

components.note: 亻 (person) shows an action by a person.
乍 (suddenly) gives the sound and the idea of making something at once.

example.pinyin: Tā zài zuòyè shang xiě míngzi.
example.english: He writes his name on the homework.
example.fact: 作 is a verb meaning 'to make, do', in 工作 (work), 作业 (homework), 作用 (effect), 作者 (author) and 作为 (as). It is mostly used in formal compounds, whereas 做 is the casual form for 'to do'.

components.note: 忄 (heart) shows an inner nature.
生 (shēng) gives a rough sound hint and means 'born', hinting at an inborn nature.

example.english: This child has a good character.
example.fact: 性 is a suffix that turns words into abstract nouns, like 可能性 (possibility) and 重要性 (importance), and it also means 'gender' (性别) or 'nature' (个性).

components.note: 走 (to walk) shows crossing over.
戉 (yuè) gives the sound exactly.

example.pinyin: Tiān yuè lái yuè lěng le.
example.fact: 越…越… is the 'the more … the more …' pattern: 越学越有意思 ('the more you study, the more interesting'). 越来越 + adjective means 'more and more'. 越 is also a verb, as in 超越 (surpass).

components.note: 舌 (tongue) is the organ that tastes.
甘 (sweet) is the taste on it.

example.fact: 甜 means sweet to the taste and can describe a person's voice or smile: 声音很甜, 甜蜜 (sweet, happy). 甜 is the opposite of 苦 (kǔ, bitter) and 酸.

components.note: 忄 (heart) shows a feeling.
白 (bái) gives a loose sound hint.

example.fact: 怕 can take a noun (怕狗) or a clause (怕他不来), and in speech it can also mean 'I'm afraid that…', as in 恐怕. It's more everyday than 害怕, which often takes no object.

components.note: 讠 (speech) shows words being recorded.
己 (jǐ) gives the sound; the tones are close.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jì bu zhù tā de míngzi.
example.fact: 记 is used in 记得 (remember), 记住 (commit to memory), 日记 (diary) and 记者 (reporter). 记得 and 记住 differ: 记得 describes a state, 记住 describes the effort.

components.note: 口 (mouth) marks a spoken word.
舍 (shè) gives a loose sound hint.

example.fact: 啥 is a colloquial northern way to say 什么, common in Northeastern dialect and sitcoms: 干啥 ('what are you doing?'), 啥事 ('what's up?'). In formal writing, avoid it.

components.note: Simplified from 聲, which pictured a stone chime being struck near the ear; the modern form is a much reduced version and does not break down clearly.

example.fact: 声 is the sound or voice: 声音, 大声 (loudly), 小声 (quietly) and 声调 (tone). It's also the measure word for calls and sounds: 叫了一声 ('called once').

components.note: 隹 (short-tailed bird) shows birds.
木 (tree) is where they flock together.

example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànshìjù yǒu sānshí jí.
example.english: This TV drama has thirty episodes.
example.fact: 集 is a measure word for TV episodes (第一集) and a verb meaning 'to gather': 集合 (assemble), 集中 (concentrate), 收集 (collect). It also means a market in 赶集 (go to a market fair).

components.note: 广 (a building) shows a place.
占 (zhàn) gives a rough sound hint; the finals are similar.

example.fact: 店 is a shop, with the measure word 家 (一家店). Common compounds are 商店 (shop), 书店 (bookstore), 饭店 (restaurant or hotel) and 酒店 (hotel).

components.note: 酉 (wine jar) shows strong wine.
告 (gào) gives a rough sound hint.

example.fact: 酷 originally meant 'cruel' (残酷) and 'strong' (of liquor), and today it also means 'cool', borrowed from English as a sound match. The two senses sit side by side: 酷刑 (torture) and 很酷 (very cool).

components.note: 言 (speech) shows that it's a warning in words.
敬 (jìng) gives the sound; the tones and finals are close.

example.fact: 警 forms 警察 (police), 报警 (call the police) and 警告 (warning). 警察 is the person, while 警 alone is the shorter spoken form for 'police' only in compounds like 警车.

components.note: 舟 (boat) is the left side.

example.pinyin: Wǒmen zuò chuán qù nàge dǎo.
example.english: We take a boat to that island.
example.fact: 船 takes the measure word 条 for small boats and 艘 for ships, and 坐船 is the verb phrase 'to travel by boat'. Compounds include 轮船 (steamship), 飞船 (spaceship) and 船长 (captain).

components.note: 亻 (person) is the giver.
寸 (hand, here measuring) shows the hand passing over something.

example.fact: 付 means to pay and is used in 付款 (payment), 付钱, 支付 (pay) and 付出 (devote). When paying a bill, 买单 is the casual way and 结账 is the other common phrase.

components.note: 辶 (walking) shows going all around.
扁 (biǎn) gives the sound; only the tone differs.

example.english: Please say it one more time.
example.fact: 遍 is a measure word for repeating a whole action from start to finish: 说一遍, 看一遍. It differs from 次 (cì), which counts any occurrence. 遍 also means 'everywhere', as in 遍地 and 走遍.

components.note: 止 (foot) shows one foot.
The lower part is another foot reversed, so the pair shows walking one step after the other.

example.fact: 步 is a step in a literal and abstract sense: 步行 (walk), 进步 (progress), 一步一步 (step by step) and 第一步 (first step). 散步 is 'to take a stroll'.

components.note: Picture of a figure with a big head and a tail-like shape, which stands for a spirit.

example.fact: 鬼 is a ghost and also a suffix for people with a bad habit: 酒鬼 (drunkard), 懒鬼 (lazy bones) and 小鬼 (little rascal, affectionate). 鬼 also appears in 鬼节 (Ghost Festival, in the seventh lunar month).

components.note: 亻 (person) shows that it is about a person.
The right part is a stack of pieces whose combined meaning is not clear, so it is best learned as a whole.

example.fact: 傻 is 'silly' in a mild and sometimes affectionate way: 傻瓜 (fool), 装傻 (play dumb), 傻笑 (laugh foolishly). It's softer than 笨 (bèn, dull, slow-witted).

components.note: 犭 (dog) is an animal radical, hinting at wild behaviour.
㔾 (a kneeling person) gives a loose sound hint.

example.fact: 犯 means to commit or to violate: 犯错 (make a mistake), 犯法 (break the law) and 犯人 (criminal). It also appears in 犯困 (feel sleepy), a colloquial phrase.

components.note: 扌 (hand) shows the action.
乃 (nǎi) gives a rough sound hint.

example.fact: 扔 is the colloquial 'throw' and 'throw away': 扔掉 (throw out) and 扔球 (throw a ball). It is more casual than 丢 and 投.

components.note: 礻 (altar) shows a religious ritual.
兄 (elder brother, here a person with an open mouth) shows someone speaking prayers at the altar.

example.fact: 祝 is used in set greetings: 祝你好运 (good luck), 祝福 (blessings) and 祝贺 (congratulations). The pattern is 祝 + person + wish.

components.note: 十 (here a weapon-like cross) sits on top.
儿 (legs, a person) is the lower part; the pair is read as someone taking on and subduing a challenge.

example.fact: 克 is the gram in modern use (一克), and it means 'to overcome' in 克服 (overcome) and 攻克. In 巧克力 (chocolate) it is just a sound.

components.note: Square picture of an open mouth.

example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā yǒu wǔ kǒu rén.
example.english: There are five people in my family.
example.fact: 口 is the mouth and the measure word for family members (三口之家, a family of three), for mouthfuls and for things with openings like wells. It appears in 口语 (spoken language), 出口 (exit) and 人口 (population).

components.note: 耳 (ear) is the left side.
阝 (a city or place shape) is the right-hand part; the sound link to yē is loose.

example.fact: 耶 is mostly seen in the Chinese name of Jesus, 耶稣, and in 耶路撒冷 (Jerusalem). As a literary particle (耶, yé) it marks a question, but that use is archaic.

excludeSuggestion: Occurs almost only in transliterated names (耶稣, 耶路撒冷).

components.note: Circle with a mark inside, an old picture of the sun, squared off in modern script.

example.pinyin: Jīntiān shì jǐ yuè jǐ rì?
example.fact: 日 is formal for 'day' in dates (五月三日) while in speech people say 号 (hào). It is also the short name for Japan (日本) and in 日子 (days, life).

components.note: Built from 一 and 厶 over a 王-like shape; the parts do not clearly explain 'lose', so it is best learned as a whole.

example.fact: 丢 means to lose or throw away: 丢了 (lost), 丢人 / 丢脸 (to lose face). It is the casual word for losing things, whereas 失 appears in 失去.

components.note: 令 (command) shows the order given.
口 (mouth) is the voice that gives the order.

example.fact: 命 means both 'life' (生命, 救命) and 'fate' (命运, 算命), and 'order' (命令). The word 命 in 救命 ('help!') is a common shout.

components.note: 夕 (evening) is the left part.
卜 (divination) is the right part; the combination is usually explained as divining at an unusual hour, hence 'outside the norm'.

example.english: He is waiting for you outside.
example.fact: 外 is the opposite of 内 and 里: 外面 (outside), 外国 (foreign country), 外语 (foreign language) and 另外 (in addition). 外 can also be 'wife's side', in 外婆 and 外公.
